text: Education begins with stories, since children hear stories before they ever train their bodies (Republic 376e–377a). The founders of the city must therefore supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates lays down two laws governing what may be said about the gods. The first is that God is good, and because he is good he is the cause of good things only (379b–c). Nothing good can cause harm. The evils of the world far outnumber the goods, and for those evils some cause other than God must be found. The second law is that God neither changes nor deceives. Whatever is in the best condition is least altered by outside forces, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse (380e–381c). Three kinds of story fall under these laws and must be excluded: Homer's two jars standing at the threshold of Zeus (379d), any poet who blames a god for the ruin of a household, and the old tales of gods who change their shape. The lie that gods and humans hate most is the lie in the soul rather than the spoken lie, and Socrates defines it as being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself (382a–b). A god has no such lie within him. Nor does a god have any motive to put one in anyone else's soul.
